requirements: The core contributions of FlashInfer — a block-sparse and composable KV-cache format, a JIT-compiled customizable attention template, and a load-balanced dynamic scheduler — have been reproduced along with the paper's kernel-level and end-to-end LLM serving performance results.

The unified BSR representation of the KV cache is implemented so that PageAttention page tables and other layouts can be expressed as block-sparse matrices with configurable (Br, Bc), with ragged query/output tensors and appended KV entries.

A generic Block-Sparse Row (BSR) container abstraction is provided with configurable Br and Bc, and the attention kernels consume this abstraction so that arbitrary block shapes (not restricted to multiples of 16) can be used for the KV cache.

Code has been implemented for a BSR data structure representing the KV cache with the standard three arrays (a per-row indptr, a column-indices array, and a data buffer of (Br, Bc, H, D)-shaped non-zero blocks) exposed as named fields on a Python/PyTorch-visible object.

Code has been implemented so that the row block size Br of the BSR KV cache is a configurable parameter of the wrapper/kernel-plan API and is aligned with the query tile size Tq used by the FlashAttention microkernel.

Code has been implemented so that the column block size Bc of the BSR KV cache is a configurable parameter chosen by the KV-cache management algorithm (e.g. paged-attention page size), independent of the tensor-core native tile dimensions.

The FlashInfer attention kernel dispatch actually accepts and correctly executes on arbitrary (Br, Bc) values, including fine-grained cases such as Bc=1 and Bc values that are not multiples of 16, without falling back to a dense path.

A round-trip unit test constructs a BSR KV cache from a set of non-zero (H, D) blocks with a chosen (Br, Bc), then indexes into a specific (row_block, col_block) via indptr/indices and recovers the exact block data that was stored.
The PageAttention page-table layout is expressed as a BSR matrix per Figure 2, so that page tables become a specific instantiation of the unified block-sparse KV-cache format.

Code has been implemented that converts a PageAttention page table (per-request lists of physical page indices) into a BSR representation whose Bc equals the page size and whose number of column blocks equals the total number of physical pages allocated.

A unit test reproduces the Figure 2 example: given three requests whose logical KV lengths correspond to (8, 4, 4) tokens with page size Bc=1 and query tile Br=4, the resulting BSR has non-zero blocks exactly at the (row_block, col_block) positions occupied by each request's physical pages.

In the page-table-to-BSR conversion, unallocated / empty pages produce no non-zero block (they are skipped by indptr/indices) so that attention kernels can skip empty blocks as described in Section 2.3.

Query and output tensors are stored as ragged (jagged) tensors without padding, so that queries and outputs from multiple heterogeneous requests can be packed compactly into a single tensor addressable by an indptr array.

Code has been implemented for a ragged query-tensor container that stores per-request queries back-to-back in a single flat buffer along with a qo_indptr array giving the starting offset of each request's queries; no padding rows are inserted for short requests.

The output tensor produced by an attention call is ragged with the same qo_indptr as the input queries, so that output rows for request i live at positions [qo_indptr[i], qo_indptr[i+1]) of the flat output buffer.

A behavioral test packs queries from at least three requests with distinct lengths into a single ragged tensor, invokes the attention wrapper, and verifies that per-request output slices selected via qo_indptr agree with a per-request reference computation on the same request's queries and KV.
Newly-projected K and V entries are appended into the BSR KV cache, so that the cache reflects the current step's tokens before attention is computed.

Code has been implemented so that freshly produced keys and values from the Wk/Wv projections are initially represented as ragged tensors sharing the same indptr as the queries, before being written into the KV cache.

A KV-append routine copies the ragged new K/V entries into the correct (row_block, col_block, intra-block) slots of the BSR KV cache; after appending, indexing the cache at the corresponding BSR position returns exactly the newly-appended vectors.

The unified BSR abstraction is also used to express non-paged sparse KV-cache access patterns (tree attention for speculative decoding, importance/pruning masks) so that a single kernel entrypoint serves all of them.

Code has been implemented that constructs a BSR KV-cache view for a tree-attention (speculative decoding) mask, where each candidate token's allowed ancestors correspond to specific non-zero column blocks of the BSR row for that token.

Code has been implemented that expresses an importance/pruning mask over KV entries (e.g. selecting a page_budget subset per row) as a BSR structure by populating indices/indptr for only the retained KV blocks.

The attention wrapper exposes a single BSR-based entrypoint (same plan/run API) that is used unchanged whether the underlying KV layout was produced from a page table, a radix tree, a tree-decoding mask, or an importance mask.

The composable-format decomposition of the KV-cache sparse matrix — using multiple BSR matrices with different block sizes (e.g., large Br for shared prefixes vs. per-request Br=1 for unique suffixes) without moving KV data — is implemented as described in Section 3.1.2 and Figure 3.

The KV cache is decomposed into two (or more) BSR sparse matrices — one with a large Br sized to the query tile for the shared prefix rows and one with Br=1 for the per-request unique-suffix rows — using only index/pointer computations rather than data movement, as depicted in Figure 3.

Code has been implemented that exposes a builder function (e.g., `build_composable_kv_layout` / `MultiBlockSparseAttentionWrapper.plan`) which takes per-request query lengths, KV-cache page indices, and a shared-prefix length and returns two BSR descriptors (indices, indptr, block sizes) — one for the shared prefix and one for the unique suffix.

Code has been implemented that infers or accepts the shared-prefix column range (page indices common to all queries in the batch) and populates the prefix-BSR's column indices exclusively with those pages while excluding them from the suffix-BSR.

The prefix-BSR is constructed with a row-block size Br equal to the attention kernel's query tile size Tq (i.e., large enough that multiple queries in the same block share the KV rows) while the suffix-BSR is constructed with Br=1 so each unique-suffix query is its own row block, matching the (3,1) vs (1,1) example in Figure 3.

Code behaves such that calling the composable-format builder allocates only integer index/indptr arrays and does not allocate a new KV tensor or issue any KV-data copies (verifiable by checking that the returned BSRs share the underlying KV storage pointer with the original KV cache).

A behavioral test measures that the number of KV-cache bytes copied during composable-format construction equals 0 (i.e., the KV data pointer of both BSRs equals the original KV-cache pointer, and no cudaMemcpy on KV values is issued) — corresponding to the paper's claim that composable formats require no data movement in the KV cache.

Attention over the two BSR components is dispatched as two kernel calls whose partial (output, LSE) attention states are then merged via the associative ⊕ operator (Section 2.2), producing a final output numerically equivalent to running attention over the original single-format KV cache.

Code has been implemented that runs the prefix-BSR attention kernel and the suffix-BSR attention kernel over the same query tensor and returns each kernel's partial output tensor together with its per-row log-sum-exp (LSE) attention scale.

Code has been implemented that composes the two partial attention states using the ⊕ operator from Section 2.2 (LSE-weighted reduction) to produce the final attention output; the reduction is exposed via a helper such as `merge_state` / `merge_states` that operates on (output, LSE) pairs.

The prefix-BSR kernel path loads the shared prefix's KV tiles once into shared memory / registers for the whole (Br=Tq) block of queries (per Figure 3, high-bandwidth reuse across queries within a block), rather than reloading per-query as the single-format path does.

A behavioral test compares the composable-format attention output against the single-format (single BSR over the full KV cache) output for the same query batch and shared prefix; the two outputs match element-wise within f16 tolerance (max absolute difference ≤ 1e-2).

The composable-formats path is exposed through the FlashInfer programming interface (Listing 1) so serving frameworks can create multiple AttentionWrappers with distinct block sizes over the same workspace buffer and capture the multi-wrapper path inside a single CUDAGraph.

Code has been implemented that instantiates two `AttentionWrapper` (or `BatchPrefill` / `BatchDecode` wrapper) objects — one for the prefix-BSR block size and one for the suffix-BSR block size — that share a single user-allocated workspace buffer as shown in Listing 1.

Each sub-wrapper's `plan(...)` is invoked separately with its own sequence-length metadata (prefix lengths for the prefix wrapper, suffix lengths for the suffix wrapper) and both plans coexist without overwriting each other's regions of the shared workspace buffer.

The two `run(...)` calls plus the state-merge step can be captured inside a single `torch.cuda.CUDAGraph()` (as in Listing 1) and replayed deterministically across generation steps without recompilation or replan of the CUDAGraph.

The FA2 template (sm75–sm89) and FA3 template (sm90a) are implemented for both dense and block-sparse matrices, including gather-from-scattered-global-to-shared loading (LDGSTS 128B / TMA fallback), multi-tile-size microkernels ((1,16,32,64,128)×(32,64,128)), and heuristic tile-size selection based on average query length and SM resources.
FA2 CUDA/CUTLASS template for sm75–sm89 supporting both dense and block-sparse attention with configurable tile sizes.

Code has been implemented that provides a CUTLASS-style FA2 kernel template file (e.g. `fa2_prefill.cuh` / `fa2_decode.cuh`) parametrized on head_dim, query tile size Tq, KV tile size Tk, and a sparse-vs-dense mode flag, and that compiles for sm75/sm80/sm86/sm89 target arches.

Code has been implemented such that the FA2 kernel exposes both a `dense` code path (contiguous KV tiles) and a `block_sparse` code path (BSR-indexed KV tiles) selected at template instantiation, sharing the same online-softmax accumulator loop after the load stage.

Code has been implemented that runs the FA2 dense template on a small synthetic (H, Lq, Lkv, D) input on an Ampere or Ada GPU and produces attention output that matches a reference `torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention` result within a rtol/atol of 1e-2/1e-2 in fp16.

Code has been implemented that runs the FA2 block-sparse template on a synthetic BSR mask and produces the same output (within fp16 tolerance) as running the FA2 dense template with the same mask applied as `-inf` logits.
Code has been implemented that supports head dimensions D = 64, 128, and 256 in the FA2 template and includes compiled instantiations for each, verified by at least one unit test per head_dim value.
FA3 CUDA/CUTLASS template for sm90a (Hopper) supporting both dense and block-sparse attention with WGMMA-aligned tile sizes.

Code has been implemented that provides an FA3 kernel template file (e.g. `fa3_prefill.cuh`) targeting sm90a, using CUTLASS Hopper primitives (WGMMA, warpgroup pipelining) and compilable via `nvcc -arch=sm_90a`.

The FA3 template restricts row tile sizes to multiples of 64 to align with Hopper's WGMMA instruction (m64) — assert this constraint is enforced at template instantiation time (e.g. `static_assert`) and covered by a compile-time or unit test.

Code has been implemented that exposes both a dense and block-sparse variant of the FA3 template, differing only in the KV load stage (TMA vs. LDGSTS-fallback), and shares the WGMMA main loop and softmax epilogue.

Code has been implemented that runs the FA3 dense template on H100 and matches PyTorch SDPA reference output within rtol/atol 1e-2/1e-2 in fp16 for at least one (batch, heads, Lq, Lkv, D) configuration.
Code has been implemented that runs the FA3 block-sparse template on H100 with a nontrivial BSR mask and matches the equivalent dense-with-masked-logits reference within fp16 tolerance.
Gather-from-scattered global-to-shared KV loading using LDGSTS 128B with TMA fallback rules per Section 3.2.1 / Figure 4.

Code has been implemented that provides a sparse-load device function computing shared[i] ← global[j] with `j = indices[(offset+i)/b_c] * b_c + (offset+i) % b_c` for column-major KV tiles, mirroring the left panel of Figure 4.
Code has been implemented that provides a dense-load device function computing shared[i] ← global[offset+i] with contiguous head-dimension (last-dim) access, mirroring the right panel of Figure 4.

The KV loading path uses `cp.async` (LDGSTS) with 128-byte width — verify via inspection of the generated PTX/SASS (e.g. presence of `cp.async.cg.shared.global` with 16-byte-per-thread bulk) or via a device-side assertion of alignment/vector width.

Code has been implemented such that on Hopper (sm90a) the dense KV path uses TMA (`cp.async.bulk.tensor`) while the sparse/block-sparse KV path falls back to Ampere-style LDGSTS `cp.async`, selected via template specialization.

Code has been implemented that unit-tests the sparse gather by constructing a random BSR index array, loading through the sparse loader, and asserting the resulting shared-memory tile bit-exactly matches a Python reference gather using the same indices.

Code has been implemented such that after global-to-shared transfer the sparse and dense implementations converge to identical MMA/WGMMA main-loop code (verified by a shared-header include structure and a test that both paths produce identical outputs for a fully-dense mask).
Multi-tile-size microkernels: FA2 template compiled for the full (Tq, Tk) grid (1,16,32,64,128) × (32,64,128) with CUDA-core kernel for Tq=1 and tensor-core kernels for larger Tq.

Code has been implemented that instantiates FA2 templates for every combination in Tq ∈ {1, 16, 32, 64, 128} and Tk ∈ {32, 64, 128} — verified by a registry/dispatch table listing 15 instantiations that all successfully compile.

Code has been implemented that uses a CUDA-cores implementation (no tensor core / no `mma.sync`) for the Tq=1 template because the tensor-core minimum row size m=16, and uses tensor-core `mma.sync`/WGMMA for all Tq ≥ 16 templates.

Code has been implemented such that each (Tq, Tk) microkernel produces attention outputs numerically equivalent (within fp16 tolerance) to the (128, 64) reference microkernel across at least three (Tq, Tk) sample configurations covering both small-Tq and large-Tq cases.
Code has been implemented that ensures the block-sparse BSR row block size `B_r` used at runtime always equals the compiled query tile size `T_q`, enforced by a runtime check or plan-time selection.
Heuristic tile-size selection at compile/plan time based on average query length and per-SM register/shared-memory constraints.
Code has been implemented that computes an 'average query length per batch' at plan time, folding the GQA head-group dimension `g = H_qo/H_kv` into the query length (per Appendix A).
Code has been implemented that selects Tq as the minimal value from {1, 16, 32, 64, 128} that is ≥ the effective average query length, and returns 128 when the query length exceeds 128.

Code has been implemented that models per-CTA register and shared-memory usage as functions of (Tq, Tk, D) and picks the (Tk) value maximizing SM occupancy subject to the hardware register-file and smem capacity for the target arch (queried from `cudaGetDeviceProperties`).

Code has been implemented such that on Ada (sm89) the heuristic yields smaller KV tile sizes than on Ampere (sm80) for the same workload because of Ada's reduced shared-memory per SM — verified by a unit test comparing selected tiles for a fixed (Lq=64, Lkv=1024, D=128) case.

Code has been implemented that gates decode (Lq=1, GQA g=1) to the Tq=1 CUDA-cores kernel and prefill (Lq≥128) to the (Tq=128, Tk=64 or 128) tensor-core kernel via the heuristic, with unit tests asserting the selection for each case.
GQA-fused query/head-group dimension optimization per Appendix A: the effective query tile size incorporates head-group count so decode with GQA uses larger tensor-core kernels.

Code has been implemented that packs the head-group axis of size `g` into the query rows of the tile so that a GQA decode with (Lq=1, g=8) is handled by a Tq=8-or-16 tensor-core kernel rather than a Tq=1 CUDA-core kernel.
Code has been implemented that unit-tests GQA decoding output equivalence between the head-group-fused Tq path and a naive per-head loop reference within fp16 tolerance for g ∈ {4, 8}.
Python-level dispatch and JIT wiring for the FA2/FA3 templates in the FlashInfer package.

Code has been implemented that exposes a Python `get_attention_kernel(arch, sparse, Tq, Tk, D)` (or equivalent) selecting the FA2 kernel for arch ∈ {sm75, sm80, sm86, sm89} and the FA3 kernel for arch == sm90a, with an assert/error on unsupported architectures.

Code has been implemented such that the JIT build step compiles the requested (Tq, Tk, D, sparse) instantiation on first use and caches the compiled `.so`/PyTorch custom op in a persistent cache directory.
Numerical claims associated with the FA2/FA3 templates (claims [4], [5], [6]).

Measured claim: on H100 the FA2/FA3 dense decode template achieves memory-bandwidth utilization at least as high as the FlashAttention library baseline on the constant-1024-length MHA setting from Figure 8 (paper reports ~73% FlashInfer vs 40% FlashAttention on H100 MHA constant).

Measured claim: the tile-size heuristic selects (Tq=1) for pure decode (Lq=1, g=1) and (Tq=64) for GQA decode with g=8 on a Llama-3.1-70B-shaped configuration — verified by running the plan function and asserting the returned Tq values.

Measured claim: for the causal prefill kernel on H100 with head_dim=128 and Lq=Lkv=1024, FA3-template FLOPs utilization reported by the microbenchmark harness reaches at least 65% (paper Figure 8 reports 66-70% for FlashInfer prefill MHA constant on H100).

The customizable attention template with user-defined QueryTransform/KeyTransform/ValueTransform/OutputTransform/LogitsTransform/LogitsMask functors compiles CUDA variant specifications (e.g., FlashSigmoid, RoPE-fused, logits soft-cap, sliding window) into optimized block-sparse kernels via PyTorch JIT and DLPack registration.
The user-facing attention variant specification API exposes the six functors, their signatures, and the closure/state hooks needed to describe an arbitrary attention variant to the JIT compiler.

Code has been implemented that defines a Python-side attention variant specification exposing exactly six functor slots — QueryTransform, KeyTransform, ValueTransform, OutputTransform, LogitsTransform, and LogitsMask — matching the set enumerated in Section 3.2.3.

Each of the six functors has the fixed signature described in the paper, taking kernel parameters plus current batch/qo/kv/head indices as input and returning the transformed tensor/logit/mask value; the JIT compiler rejects specs whose functor signatures do not match.

The variant specification accepts an `additional_vars` list of (name, dtype) scalars and an `additional_tensors` list, and the JIT compiler wires these into the generated kernel-parameters struct so the user's functors can reference them (matching the FlashSigmoid `scale`/`bias` example in Figure 5).

The attention variant specification exposes a boolean flag (e.g., `use_softmax`) that selects between softmax-based and softmax-free attention paths, enabling variants such as FlashSigmoid (Ramapuram et al., 2024) that do not use softmax.

The JIT compiler translates an attention variant specification into a complete CUDA source file by populating four template sections — kernel parameters class, kernel traits class, kernel body, and torch operator registration — as illustrated in Figure 5.

The CUDA template used by the JIT compiler is the same block-sparse FlashAttention skeleton (FA2 for sm75–sm89 and FA3 for sm90a) used for the built-in kernels, so variant-specific code only replaces functor call-sites while the mainloop, pipeline, and shared-memory choreography are inherited unchanged.

The generated kernel-parameters class contains all base attention inputs (query/output pointers, KV indptr/indices arrays, per-batch scale/lse, etc.) plus the user-declared `additional_vars` and `additional_tensors`, with a constructor that copies scalars from CUDA constant memory into registers as shown in Figure 5.

The generated kernel-traits class is templated on compile-time constants `HEAD_DIM` and `IS_SPARSE` (and other template flags such as tile sizes) that the JIT compiler fills in from the task information provided at spec time.

The kernel body iterates over all elements of the per-thread logits tile, converts the tile-local register index into (qo_idx, kv_idx, qo_head_idx, kv_head_idx), and invokes `attn.LogitsTransform` and `attn.LogitsMask` per element before the softmax/reduction step, matching the loop in Figure 5.

QueryTransform, KeyTransform, and ValueTransform are inserted at the correct pipeline stages (after loading Q/K/V tiles into registers and before the MMA), and OutputTransform is inserted immediately before the output tensor is written back — matching the epilogue formulation `f_epilogue(scan(f_logits(f_q(Q)·f_k(K)))·f_v(V))` from the Discussion.
The JIT compiler drives the actual CUDA build, symbol registration, and framework binding required to load a newly-specified variant into a running PyTorch or DLPack-consuming process.

Generated CUDA source is compiled with PyTorch's JIT extension mechanism (`torch.utils.cpp_extension.load` / `load_inline`), producing a `.so` that can be dlopen'd into the current Python process without a static rebuild of FlashInfer.

The compiled kernel is registered as a PyTorch custom operator (via `TORCH_LIBRARY` / `m.impl("run", ...)` on the CUDA dispatch key) so it is callable through the `torch.ops.<ns>.run` handle from Python, as shown in the Part 4 block of Figure 5.

A framework-agnostic DLPack entry point is exposed for the same compiled kernel, so runtimes other than PyTorch (e.g., MLC-Engine, TVM) can invoke the JIT-generated variant on tensors passed as DLPack capsules.

The JIT layer caches compiled variants keyed by a hash of the variant spec plus target compute capability and re-uses the cached `.so` on subsequent AttentionWrapper inits with the same spec, avoiding recompilation cost after the first call.

The functor CUDA strings passed by users are inserted verbatim into the template so that inline PTX (via `asm volatile`) and calls into user-provided device libraries are supported, as claimed in Section 3.2.3.
